   139  /*
   140   * Sanitize
   141   *
   142   *
   143   * === Introduction ===
   144   *
   145   * The sanitize machinery is at the core of our zero-cost font loading.  We
   146   * mmap() font file into memory and create a blob out of it.  Font subtables
   147   * are returned as a readonly sub-blob of the main font blob.  These table
   148   * blobs are then sanitized before use, to ensure invalid memory access does
   149   * not happen.  The toplevel sanitize API use is like, eg. to load the 'head'
   150   * table:
   151   *
   152   *   hb_blob_t *head_blob = hb_sanitize_context_t ().reference_table<OT::head> (face);
   153   *
   154   * The blob then can be converted to a head table struct with:
   155   *
   156   *   const head *head_table = head_blob->as<head> ();
   157   *
   158   * What the reference_table does is, to call hb_face_reference_table() to load
   159   * the table blob, sanitize it and return either the sanitized blob, or empty
   160   * blob if sanitization failed.  The blob->as() function returns the null
   161   * object of its template type argument if the blob is empty.  Otherwise, it
   162   * just casts the blob contents to the desired type.
   163   *
   164   * Sanitizing a blob of data with a type T works as follows (with minor
   165   * simplification):
   166   *
   167   *   - Cast blob content to T*, call sanitize() method of it,
   168   *   - If sanitize succeeded, return blob.
   169   *   - Otherwise, if blob is not writable, try making it writable,
   170   *     or copy if cannot be made writable in-place,
   171   *   - Call sanitize() again.  Return blob if sanitize succeeded.
   172   *   - Return empty blob otherwise.
   173   *
   174   *
   175   * === The sanitize() contract ===
   176   *
   177   * The sanitize() method of each object type shall return true if it's safe to
   178   * call other methods of the object, and false otherwise.
   179   *
   180   * Note that what sanitize() checks for might align with what the specification
   181   * describes as valid table data, but does not have to be.  In particular, we
   182   * do NOT want to be pedantic and concern ourselves with validity checks that
   183   * are irrelevant to our use of the table.  On the contrary, we want to be
   184   * lenient with error handling and accept invalid data to the extent that it
   185   * does not impose extra burden on us.
   186   *
   187   * Based on the sanitize contract, one can see that what we check for depends
   188   * on how we use the data in other table methods.  Ie. if other table methods
   189   * assume that offsets do NOT point out of the table data block, then that's
   190   * something sanitize() must check for (GSUB/GPOS/GDEF/etc work this way).  On
   191   * the other hand, if other methods do such checks themselves, then sanitize()
   192   * does not have to bother with them (glyf/local work this way).  The choice
   193   * depends on the table structure and sanitize() performance.  For example, to
   194   * check glyf/loca offsets in sanitize() would cost O(num-glyphs).  We try hard
   195   * to avoid such costs during font loading.  By postponing such checks to the
   196   * actual glyph loading, we reduce the sanitize cost to O(1) and total runtime
   197   * cost to O(used-glyphs).  As such, this is preferred.
   198   *
   199   * The same argument can be made re GSUB/GPOS/GDEF, but there, the table
   200   * structure is so complicated that by checking all offsets at sanitize() time,
   201   * we make the code much simpler in other methods, as offsets and referenced
   202   * objectes do not need to be validated at each use site.
   203   */
